text: Darwinia pinifolia is a flowering plant in the family Myrtaceae and is native exclusively to the southwest of Western Australia. It grows as a low, spreading to prostrate shrub, reaching a height of 10–50 cm (3.9–19.7 in), with numerous branches. The plant has linear leaves that are nearly round to triangular in cross-section, measuring about 12 mm (0.47 in) in length and lacking a distinct stalk. Its flowers are erect, ranging in color from red to purple, and are arranged in dense heads at the ends of branches, surrounded by egg-shaped or spatula-shaped bracteoles that are shorter than the flowers. The sepal tube is approximately 6.5 mm (0.26 in) long and features broadly egg-shaped lobes that are about as long as the petals. Flowering takes place from September to February. The species was first formally described in 1839 by John Lindley, who named it Hedaroma pinifolium in A Sketch of the Vegetation of the Swan River Colony. In 1865, George Bentham reclassified it as Pimelea pinifolia in the Journal of the Linnean Society, Botany. The specific epithet "pinifolia" means "pine-leaved." It is commonly found in sandy soils within winter-wet areas of the Geraldton Sandplains, Jarrah Forest, and Swan Coastal Plain bioregions of south-western Western Australia.
